3.title: Checks come first
3.summary: Arjun's 50.Qg7 went for f7 and let Black's queen and rook start checking.
3.analysis: Arjun's king on h3 had little cover, and Black's queen and rook were both already in his camp. 50.Qf4! brought the queen back to defend and took the e4-square away from Black's rook (0.00 in the deep check). 50.Qg7, going after the f7-pawn, took the queen out of the defence, and the checks began: 50...Qh1+ 51.Kg4 Re4+ 52.Rf4 Qd1+. The king was driven up the board and material soon dropped (−6.0). IM Prin Laohawirapap of Thailand converted, one of the upsets of the first round.
3.prevent: When both enemy heavy pieces are near your king, count their checks before starting your own attack. A defensive queen move that covers the key checking squares is often the only move.

12.title: The King's Indian bishop wakes up
12.summary: After ...exf4 opened the long diagonal, 29.axb5 allowed ...Bd4+, forking king and rook.
12.analysis: When Black recaptured 28...exf4, the e5-pawn left the long diagonal and the bishop on g7 could suddenly reach d4. From there it checks the king on g1 and hits the rook on a1 at the same time, and taking it with Qxd4 cxd4 costs White the queen. 29.Bc3! blocks the diagonal and offers a trade (0.00 in the deep check). White took on b5 with 35 seconds left, and after 29...Bd4+ 30.Rf2 Bxa1 Black was a clean exchange up (−3.8).
12.prevent: When a pawn trade opens a long diagonal toward your king, check every square the enemy bishop can now reach with check. A check that also hits a loose rook is a fork waiting to happen, so block the diagonal or move the rook first.

318.title: Four seconds in a won pawn ending
318.summary: 58.Ke4 turned a forced win into a draw. 58.Kc6 outflanked the black king.
318.analysis: A king-and-pawn ending that White wins by force. The black king on e7 guards d6 and e6 but has to stay near its f6-pawn, so White goes round it: 58.Kc6! Ke8 59.Kd6 and 60.Ke6, and the f6-pawn falls (the deep check shows a forced win). 58.Ke4 stepped back and let Black's king hold everything; the engine calls the position a dead draw (0.00). It was played in four seconds with more than forty minutes on the clock. The score records 1-0 straight after 58.Ke4, so Black never got to prove the draw.
318.prevent: In king-and-pawn endings one tempo decides, so calculate before every king move, however easy it looks. Know the key squares and the outflanking idea, and use the time when the clock allows it.

1772.title: One knight move, two lines opened
1772.summary: 37...Nf5 cleared the h2–c7 diagonal and allowed 38.Ne6+, winning Black's queen.
1772.analysis: Black's king was out on g5, and the knight on d6 was blocking the diagonal between White's queen on h2 and Black's queen on c7. 37...Nf5 moved it. 38.Ne6+! forked the king and queen, so Black had to take with 38...Rxe6. Then 39.gxh4+ captured with check and cleared g3 at the same time, and after 39...Nxh4 40.Qxc7 the queen went (+4.0 in the deep check). Stepping the king off the knight's check square with 37...Kh6 or 37...Kf6 kept the balance (0.00). It was played in 43 seconds with half an hour left.
1772.prevent: When your king is in the open, look at every enemy check, especially knight checks that also hit your queen. And when a piece leaves a square, ask which line it was blocking.

1774.title: A king step onto a checking square
1774.summary: With 49 seconds left, 68...Kh6 allowed 69.Bg7+, and the checks that followed won the knight.
1774.analysis: White's pawn on f7 is one step from queening, held back by Black's knight covering f8. 68...Kh5! kept the balance (+0.2 in the deep check). 68...Kh6 allowed 69.Bg7+!, a check from a square where the bishop is protected by the rook on g8 and also covers f8. In the deep line the king has to go back, 70.Bd4+ follows, and after 70...Kxf7 71.Rg7+ White picks up the knight on h7 (+5.3). Urkedal had 49 seconds left and spent 24. Niemann won.
1774.prevent: With an enemy pawn on the seventh rank, every check matters because it gains the tempo needed to promote. Before a king move, list the checks it allows and look for the ones that also cover the queening square.

2162.title: The square the king needed
2162.summary: Rapport's 58.Ng5 got in his own king's way. 58.Ne5 was a clean draw.
2162.analysis: Knight against knight and two pawns, and Black's pawns were not enough to win if White's king could get at them. 58.Ne5! heads for c4 and d2 while the king goes to g5, and in the deep check White wins the h-pawn and draws (0.00). 58.Ng5 put the knight on the square the king wanted and let Black's king in: 58...Kg6 59.Nf3 Kh6 60.Kg3 Ng6, and Black's pieces now protect each other and both pawns (−4.4). Four moves earlier Black had let a win slip with 54...Nf4, so the endgame changed hands twice. Cheng won.
2162.prevent: In knight endgames the king does the work. Keep your pieces off the squares your king needs, and when you're defending against pawns, go after the one furthest from the enemy king.

2166.title: Taking a pawn that was already lost
2166.summary: Wesley So's 54.Rxd3 cost the tempo that mattered. 54.Kc7 held.
2166.analysis: The d3-pawn wasn't going anywhere: the rook on d4 already stopped it. 54.Kc7! brings the king next to the c-pawn first, and the deep check calls it holdable (−0.5), because the c-pawn becomes a real runner that Black's rook has to watch. Taking at once with 54.Rxd3 let 54...Rc2 hit the c4-pawn, and after 55.Rd4 the rook was tied to its defence. With White's king stuck on the back rank, far from Black's f- and g-pawns, those two connected passers decided (−3.2). Hovhannisyan won.
2166.prevent: In rook endgames, ask which pawn matters. An enemy pawn that is doomed can wait; improving your king next to your own passed pawn usually comes first. Grabbing material that will fall anyway can hand the opponent the tempo that decides the race.

2549.title: Take the rook
2549.summary: 23...Kxf7 accepted the offer and held. 23...Be6 let White cash in.
2549.analysis: White's rook had just taken on f7, where the black king can capture it. 23...Kxf7! was the move: after 24.Qf3+ Nf4 25.Bxf4 Qxf4 26.Qxa8 Qe3+ 27.Kh1 Qxd2, White is only slightly better (+1.0 in the deep check). 23...Be6 attacked the rook instead of taking it, and White simply cashed in with 24.Rxe7+ Qxe7 25.Qf3, staying clearly ahead in material with the safer king (+3.5). It was played with just over four minutes left.
2549.prevent: When your opponent leaves a piece where you can take it, calculate the capture before looking for alternatives. Here the only question was whether the checks after 23...Kxf7 were dangerous, and they weren't.

2946.title: A spite check in a King's Indian endgame
2946.summary: One rook check cost the tempo Black needed. 68...Kd6 drew.
2946.analysis: Black's rook on a2 guards the b2-pawn and ties White's rook to the b-file, so the job was to bring the king over to support the pawn. 68...Kd6! heads for c5, c4 and c3, and in the deep check White ends up giving his rook for the b-pawn while his own pawns run, with a draw (0.00). 68...Ra4+ gains nothing: after 69.Kh3 the b2-pawn is hanging, so the rook has to go straight back with 69...Ra2. Black has spent two moves and his king is no nearer the queenside, and that was enough to lose the race (+4.0 in the deep check). It was played with under four minutes left.
2946.prevent: In rook endgames a check that gains nothing costs a tempo. Before checking, ask where the king goes and whether your rook can stay on its best square. Here the rule was to activate the king toward the passed pawn.

3359.title: A passive rook on b8
3359.summary: 28...Qd5 allowed 29.Qf4, which hit the rook and the h6-pawn together. 28...Rb5 held.
3359.analysis: White has two passed pawns on the queenside and a pawn on f5 cramping Black's king. 28...Rb5! was the active defence, hitting both a5 and f5 along the fifth rank (+0.4 in the deep check). 28...Qd5 kept the rook on b8 and allowed 29.Qf4!, which attacks the rook along the b8–h2 diagonal and the h6-pawn at the same time (+3.5). Black grabbed 29...Rxb3, but 30.Qg4+ Kf8 31.f6 brought the queen and pawn right next to the black king, with Qg7+ coming. Sindarov won.
3359.prevent: In queen endgames with an airy king, activity and king safety beat centralisation. Look for enemy queen moves that attack two things at once, especially a loose rook and a pawn near your king.

3746.title: Recapture with the right piece
3746.summary: With 36 seconds left, 34.Qxd5 allowed 34...Re1+ and a queen fork on f4.
3746.analysis: Black's bishop on d5 could be taken two ways, and the choice decided the game. 34.Nxd5 keeps the f4-square covered twice, by the knight and by the queen on f5 (−1.75 in the deep check, worse but still a game). 34.Qxd5 walked into 34...Re1+ 35.Kh2 Qf4+!, a queen fork of the king and the loose knight on f2, and White was lost (−5.8). Emre Can played it with 36 seconds on the clock, in the last round.
3746.prevent: When you have two ways to recapture, look at what each capturing piece stops guarding. Here the queen recapture left f4 open, and the knight on f2 was loose. In time trouble, recapture with the piece that keeps your king safe.

3751.title: The square that g3 gave away
3751.summary: 30.g3 let 30...Bf3+ in, and the knight fork on f3 won the exchange.
3751.analysis: All of Black's pieces have arrived on the kingside, the usual picture in the Mar del Plata, but White was still better: 30.c6 or 30.Bxg4 Qxg4 31.Nb5 kept an edge of about +1.5 to +2. 30.g3 attacks the knight on h4 but takes away the pawn that guarded f3. 30...Bf3+! 31.Bxf3 Nxf3 followed, and the knight forks the queen on e1 and the rook on g1. After 32.Qf1 Nxg1 Black was up the exchange with the attack still running (−2.7 in the deep check), and won.
3751.prevent: A pawn move in front of your king gives up the squares it used to guard. Before a move like g2-g3 with enemy pieces nearby, list the squares the pawn stops covering and check whether an enemy piece can land there with check or a threat.

4996.title: Prophylaxis before a pawn move
4996.summary: 29.h4 let 29...Bb3 chase the rook off the d-file that protected White's passed pawn.
4996.analysis: White's asset is the passed pawn on d6, backed by the queen and rook on the d-file. 29.h4, played with under five minutes left, ignored Black's only active idea: 29...Bb3!, hitting the rook on d1. The rook has to leave the d-file, and with it goes the d6-pawn's second defender (−2.7 in the deep check). 29.Qc3 was the answer: from c3 the queen covers b3, so the bishop can't come in, and the rook on d1 still guards d6 (about −0.6, holdable). In the game White held the pawn for a moment with 30.Rc1, but after 30...Qe6 and the trade on b3 Black had a passed pawn of her own and won.
4996.prevent: Before a waiting move, go through the opponent's pieces one by one and ask what each wants to do next. Here the bishop wanted b3 to chase the rook off the d-file, so covering that square came first.

5463.title: Mate in two, missed
5463.summary: 33...Qxg3+ mated in two. Black took with the knight instead and let White back into the game.
5463.analysis: Black's pieces were all pointed at the white king: queen on g6, knight on e4, bishops on c6 and c3, rook on g8. 33...Qxg3+! forces mate: the queen can't be taken because the e4-knight guards g3, the only move is 34.Kh1, and 34...Qxh3 is mate, with the rook on g8 covering g1. Black took with the knight, 33...Nxg3, in 37 seconds, and the engine rated White better afterwards (+2.6). White returned the favour at once with 34.Rd2, and Black won.
5463.prevent: When the enemy king is short of defenders, look at every check before any other move, including captures with the queen that look risky. A forcing line of two moves is quick to calculate and decides the game.

5490.title: The queen nobody took
5490.summary: After 24.a3 a4, the black queen was hanging on b4, and 25.Rf1 left it there.
5490.analysis: 24.a3 attacked the black queen on b4, and Black answered 24...a4, leaving it where it stood. The queen was simply hanging: 25.axb4 wins it, and the pawn on b4 then hits the knight on c5 as well (+6.6 in the deep check). After nearly ten minutes' thought and with almost half an hour on the clock, White played 25.Rf1, and the queen walked away with 25...Qa5. Black went on to win.
5490.prevent: When you attack a piece and it doesn't move, check whether you can simply take it before looking for anything clever. The plain capture is the first candidate, not the last.

8878.title: A knight check with the queen behind it
8878.summary: 18...Rfd8 allowed 19.Nf6+, hitting king and queen with White's rook already on h3.
8878.analysis: White's rook had swung to h3, the bishop on b1 sat behind the knight on the diagonal to h7, and the knight on e4 was one jump from f6. 18...Rfd8 put a rook opposite White's d-file but walked into 19.Nf6+!: the knight checks from f6 and attacks the queen on d5. If the king steps aside, 20.Nxd5 wins the queen; if Black takes with 19...gxf6, as in the game, 20.Qxh6 tears the kingside open and White's attack crashed through (+5.5 in the deep check). 18...Kh8 or 18...Qc4 kept the balance.
8878.prevent: When the opponent's pieces are massed in front of your king, check their forcing moves before making a routine move. A knight check that also hits your queen is exactly the kind of move to look for.
